reading.body:
Ten frontier-technology risks are being modelled for insurance before any of them has an established loss record, and several are compute risks rather than device risks.

The pattern is liability migrating toward whoever controls the compute and the model. Autonomous fleet liability moves from local operation to central infrastructure once navigation is cloud controlled. Decentralised compute networks need risk models for distributed GPU hosting where hardware security cannot be centrally assured. Brain computer interface cover attaches to software running real-time inference. Neuromorphic and optical hardware needs breakdown cover for architectures with no established failure statistics. In each case the underwritten object is a running system, not a shipped product. The largest exposure on the list, reinsurance for systemic economic disruption from an unaligned frontier system, is also the one with the least precedent to model against.

Insurance is how a risk gets priced before it gets tolerated. A line that cannot be priced gets excluded, and an exclusion moves the cost onto the operator, the balance sheet, or the public. That matters for AI because deployment at scale depends on someone being willing to carry the tail. The compute connection here is about where inference runs and who insures it, not about how much power it draws. Nothing in this data links these exposures to grid capacity, interconnection queues, or data centre construction.

What it does not cover is scale. There are no premiums, limits, carriers, or effective dates, and every source field is empty. This is a taxonomy of exposures someone is thinking about, not a measurement of how much of it is written. It cannot say which of the ten will produce claims, how often, or how large.
